Storm response briefing — Hawaiian Islands

Lala spared the coastline a landfall. It did not spare the grid, the highways, or Kaʻū.

01
The sixty-second read

What happened, what it costs, and where the work is.

  • No landfall, hurricane-grade hit. Lala peaked as a Category 1 (80 mph, 985 mb) passing about 30 miles south of Ka Lae on Saturday evening, brushed the southern Big Island with its eyewall, and was downgraded to a tropical storm at 2:00 a.m. Sunday. It was a hurricane for roughly 17 hours — all of them next to Hawaiʻi Island.
  • Water on Hawaiʻi Island, wind on Oʻahu and Maui. 33 inches of rain fell at Laupāhoehoe; a flash-flood emergency in Kaʻū swept two homes away (confirmed) and damaged or destroyed 100+ (preliminary, Gov. Green). Oʻahu logged 39–66 reported roof-damage incidents and 147 downed trees — a full day after closest approach.
  • The grid took the structural hit. HECO peaked at 250,900 customers out — about half its base — with 25 high-voltage transmission lines down; a 42-mile Hāmākua span lost multiple poles. HECO projects days for urban Oʻahu and Maui, and weeks to months for rural Big Island.
  • Kaʻū is cut off. Highway 11 collapsed near Nāʻālehu, 6–8 bridges are damaged or destroyed, and Pāhala — home of the district's only hospital — had no ground access Sunday. The Kona side is the only way in until an emergency bypass opens.
  • Recovery machinery is moving. Hilo and Kona airports reopened Sunday; all commercial ports were reopened by Monday. About 100 mainland mutual-aid line workers arrive Tuesday and work Wednesday. Joint preliminary damage assessment is underway; no Stafford Act request had been filed as of Sunday.
  • Early money signals. Statewide damage "in the hundreds of millions" and agriculture losses of $50M+ — both preliminary. The state unlocked a $100M emergency fund on August 13, before the storm arrived.
  • No confirmed storm deaths. One Big Island traffic death is disputed as to storm attribution; one recovered body is under determination. No casualty figure belongs in any client-facing material.
Bottom line — Executive General Adjusters

Severity sits in Kaʻū, frequency sits on Oʻahu. Kaʻū's swept and washed-out homes are flood-causation files inside a simultaneous eyewall wind field — expect wind-versus-water disputes on every partial loss. Only Hawaiʻi County was hurricane-warned, and most neighbor-island damage accrued Sunday, after the downgrade: hurricane-deductible applicability turns on trigger wording. Power, civil-authority, and ingress/egress interruption claims will outnumber structure claims. The 72-hour mold threshold lands Tuesday–Wednesday.

Bottom line — NorthStar operations

Stage Kona for Kaʻū, Hilo for the windward corridor. Kaʻū movements are convoy-with-road-confirmation, self-sufficient in fuel, water, and comms. Tarping Oʻahu's 39–66 reported roof-damage incidents is the highest-leverage 72-hour action. The rural outage plateau creates weeks of temporary-power and drying demand that grid restoration cannot shortcut. The Highway 11 bypass decides whether Kaʻū presents as mitigable water losses or demolition, rebuild, and mold files — track it daily.

Held apart — figures still in conflict at cutoff

Kauaʻi outages: ~863 (KIUC, Sun 7 p.m.) vs 36,000+ (Civil Beat, Sun a.m.). Oʻahu roofs: 66 (HFD joint briefing) vs 39 (AP/Civil Beat). Kaʻū bridges: 6 (mayor's aerial survey) vs 8 (Civil Beat). Carried as ranges or held apart — never averaged.

02
Storm profile & event sequence

Seventeen hours as a hurricane. Four counties of consequence.

Tropical Cyclone Lala (CP012026) never made landfall. Terrain did the damage: the eyewall's rain trained onto Mauna Loa's southern slopes while tropical-storm wind fields worked the whole chain for another full day.

80mph Peak intensity — Category 1 985 mb · Sat Aug 15, ~5–7 p.m. HST · CPHC — confirmed
~30mi Closest pass, south of Ka Lae Sat Aug 15, ~5 p.m. HST — eyewall brushed the southern Big Island
17hrs Total time at hurricane strength Sat 9 a.m. → Sun 2 a.m. HST — all within ~150 mi of Hawaiʻi Island
305mi W Last advisory position Of Honolulu · Sun 11 p.m., 60 mph — all warnings discontinued · CPHC Adv. 20

Event sequence — HST

Aug 13
Advisories begin; state moves first

CPHC opens advisories on Lala. Governor Green signs an emergency proclamation and unlocks a $100M emergency fund — before the first band arrives.

Aug 14
Pre-staging

Hawaiian Electric activates its incident response plan and stages 500+ workers. Hawaiʻi County issues its own proclamation. USCG port condition Zulu sequence begins Friday evening.

Aug 15 · 09:00
Hurricane Lala — Category 1

Hurricane Warning for Hawaiʻi County; tropical-storm warnings for Maui County, Oʻahu, and Kauaʻi. That distinction matters to deductibles later.

Aug 15 · morning–evening
Windward rivers leave their banks

The Wailuku River in Hilo rises 3.4 → 16.2 ft in 12 hours. Hilo Bayfront floods. Highway 11 begins closing segment by segment, MM 54–69.

Aug 15 · ~17:00
Closest approach — peak intensity

Eyewall passes ~30 mi south of Ka Lae at 80 mph. Mauna Kea summit records a 140-mph gust. Kaʻū takes 3–5 in/hr rain — flash-flood emergency, and two Nāʻālehu homes are confirmed swept away Saturday evening. Big Island outages hit 63,270 by 7 p.m.

Aug 16 · 02:00
Downgrade — rescues through the night

Lala weakens to a tropical storm. National Guard rescues continue in Nāʻālehu and Waiʻōhinu, including two paramedics whose vehicle was taken by the water.

Aug 16 · morning
Oʻahu transmission failures; Kaʻū confirmed severed

Statewide outages surge to 197,400 by 7 a.m. as nine Oʻahu transmission lines fail. Highway 11's collapse is reported; Pāhala is cut off. Hilo and Kona airports reopen after inspections.

Aug 16 · 11:00
Grid nadir — 250,900 out

HECO's peak: roughly half its customer base, Oʻahu alone at 173,900. Mutual aid is requested from mainland utilities.

Aug 16 · evening
Restoration gains; first damage totals

178,400 still out by 7 p.m. — Maui down to 7,000. Governor: 100+ homes damaged or destroyed and damage "in the hundreds of millions" (both preliminary). Bridge tally 6–8 — mayor's aerial survey vs Civil Beat. Shelters drop from 426 to ~100 people. JPDA begins.

Aug 16 · 23:00
All warnings discontinued

CPHC Advisory 20: Lala 305 mi west of Honolulu at 60 mph. Forecast to re-intensify well west of the state midweek — a surf problem now, not a wind problem.

Aug 17 · 08:00
Research cutoff

116,000+ customers still out (Red Cross). ~100 mainland line workers arrive Tuesday, work Wednesday. Highway 11 bypass decision pending. Next full refresh: Aug 18, 08:00 HST.

Customers without power — Hawaiian Electric territories Aug 15–17 · HECO published snapshots, HST
Read: the peak came a full day after closest approach — transmission failures, not the storm's proximity, drove the curve. The Monday point is an American Red Cross cross-check on a different customer universe, shown hollow and never averaged with HECO's series. Kauaʻi (KIUC, a separate co-op) is excluded here: its Sunday figures conflict by ~40× between sources (~863 vs 36,000+) and are held apart until KIUC publishes its own tally.
Why rural restoration takes weeks, not days

Damage is vegetation-driven and concentrated in transmission — the backbone between generation and neighborhoods. Sixteen high-voltage lines are down on Hawaiʻi Island, and a 42-mile Hāmākua span lost multiple poles and structures — which is also what keeps four independent power producers — Puna Geothermal, Hāmākua Energy, Hāwī Renewable, Pakini Nui — disconnected. Distribution crews cannot re-energize what the backbone cannot feed. Section 05 diagrams this.

The hurricane-deductible question

Lala was a hurricane for roughly 17 hours — all of it near the Big Island. Only Hawaiʻi County carried a Hurricane Warning; Maui County, Oʻahu, and Kauaʻi were under tropical-storm warnings. Most neighbor-island damage accrued Sunday, after the 2:00 a.m. downgrade — Oʻahu's outage peak came a full day after closest approach.

Whether percentage hurricane or named-storm deductibles apply outside Hawaiʻi County turns on each policy's trigger wording — warning issued, hurricane-force conditions, or named-storm. The warning map by county and the downgrade timestamp above are the evidence base. This report states the facts; it does not adjudicate wording.

Interruption claims will outnumber structure claims

  • Service interruption: 250,900 out at peak; weeks-to-months rural Big Island — spoilage and BI in outage-only zones
  • Civil authority: USCG port Zulu closures Fri–Sat; Hilo and Kona airports closed, reopened Sunday (HNL never closed); Honolulu's Monday municipal closures — all dated, all documentable
  • Ingress/egress: Pāhala businesses have access claims independent of physical damage; ~190–200 Saturday flight cancellations anchor hospitality BI
  • Contamination: brown-water advisories and a DOH leptospirosis caution make floodwater Category 3 from day one — scope accordingly

Deployment conditions — CAT logistics

  • Air: Hilo, Kona reopened Sunday; HNL never closed. Residual schedule disruption into early week
  • Sea: all commercial ports reopened after condition Zulu — barge shipping for vehicles and equipment is viable
  • Kaʻū: base operations Kona-side; Pāhala unreachable by road at last report; confirm route status before every movement
  • Lodging: no availability data published — but ~100 mainland line workers (Tue), 226 Guard, and agency field teams compress Hilo/Kona rooms. Book early
  • Power & comms: assume no grid power in rural Big Island work zones for weeks; carry satellite comms for Kaʻū; potable water and floodwater PPE required
  • Intake signals: damage portals live in all four counties; JPDA numbers plausible within 24–48 hrs; watch for the Stafford Act request
The mitigation clock — wet-out was Aug 15–16 Industry-standard water-loss timeline (IICRC-class guidance), applied to this event — not corpus data
Applied to Lala: Kaʻū and Hilo structures wetted Saturday night reach the 72-hour mark Tuesday night Aug 18; Oʻahu and Maui Sunday wet-outs reach it Wednesday Aug 19. August humidity plus no grid power — no air conditioning, no dehumidification — in exactly the wettest districts compresses the window. Structures in the weeks-long outage plateau cannot passively dry. Tarping Oʻahu's 39–66 reported roof-damage incidents is the highest-leverage 72-hour action; trailing rain lands on every roof still open, and midweek surf from re-intensification works exposed shorelines.
Two cautions for client-facing work

Casualties: no storm-attributed death is officially confirmed — one traffic death is disputed, one recovered body is under determination. Use no casualty figures. Pre-existing damage: Kaʻū and rural Hawaiʻi parcels may carry unrepaired March 2026 Kona-low flood damage (separate federal declaration) — a causation and valuation overlap on the same properties.

Staging — where we sit while the picture firms

Kona is the Kaʻū gateway — the only verified ground approach. Hilo (airport and harbor both open) bases windward and transmission-corridor work, with the Hwy 19 (MM 28) slide constraining the northern link. Kawaihae serves Kohala by sea. Kahului is Maui's working hub. Deconflict laydown with HECO's own mutual-aid staging from Tuesday. Do not stage in Kaʻū flood zones, near saturated slopes, or across unassessed bridges.

Safety posture for field crews

Treat every downed line as energized and hold a 30-foot standoff — tree work near lines is this event's signature injury mechanism. Floodwater is Category 3: leptospirosis caution, no wading, cover cuts, decontaminate. Stay out of stream corridors and gulches 48–72 hours — landslides need no new rain. Dark signals are 4-way stops. Generators run outside, 20 feet from openings. Stop-work authority applies to every person on every site.

09
Risk watchlist & open questions

What could still move — and what we simply do not know.

Re-intensification — a surf problem, not a wind problem

Lala is forecast to regain hurricane strength well west of the state by midweek. The operational effect is renewed high surf on west- and south-facing shores through about Aug 19 — coastal facilities, shoreline roads, and any marine staging. Keep crews off exposed shorelines until advisories lift.

Saturated slopes — the dominant post-storm hazard

15–35 inches fell across Big Island catchments — observation windows vary and are not yet comparable. Landslides need no new rain: the Hwy 19 slide is active, Tantalus Drive partially collapsed, and the governor warned that rains of this class bring widespread slides. Watch corridors: windward Big Island, East Maui, Oʻahu valleys, Pali Hwy, H-3, Farrington Hwy, Hawaiʻi Belt Road.

Figures most likely to move

The Kaʻū destroyed-vs-damaged split (JPDA will supersede the 100+ figure). The bridge count (6 vs 8). The Oʻahu roof tally (39 vs 66). The KIUC outage scale (~863 vs 36,000+). Casualty determinations. The NWS post-storm rainfall table, which will finally make gauge values comparable.

Coverage gaps are not all-clears

Niʻihau has zero verified reporting. Molokaʻi's East End, Lānaʻi's interior, the Hāna–Kīpahulu structural picture, and Kona-side damage detail are all thin. No sewage, fuel, or hazmat release was confirmed at cutoff — DOH environmental findings are pending, and absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.

Sources, method & media clearance

How to read this report — and what you may republish.

Confidence labels, as used throughout

ConfirmedPrimary agency or utility release, or multiple independent primary sources
CorroboratedMultiple secondary sources agree; primary confirmation pending
PreliminaryEarly official estimate expected to be superseded — the 100+ homes figure is the example
Single-sourceOne outlet only; treat as unverified until matched
DisputedSources actively conflict — carried as a range or held apart, never averaged

Figures keep their as-of timestamps. Snapshots from different hours are never merged; conflicting tallies are shown side by side. Where the record is silent, the report says so instead of filling the gap.

Media & imagery clearance for republication

Class A — cleared HDOT / Hawaiʻi County Civil Defense official imagery (road clearing, flood response). Public domain government work. Credit: "Photo courtesy of the Hawaiʻi Department of Transportation / Hawaiʻi County Civil Defense"
Class C — restricted Wire-agency photography (AFP/Getty and similar). Commercial license required — do not republish on LinkedIn or client materials
Class D — link only Editorial and community photos (Civil Beat staff and courtesy images). Link to the story; do not re-host the asset

No third-party photography is embedded in this report. The cover visual and island relief tiles are NorthStar-produced illustrative renderings — not satellite, survey, or event imagery — and are cleared for distribution with the file, which remains clearance-safe to forward.
